pig-collagen.summary: Collagen from pig skin used in Korean sheet masks, creams and supplements for plumper, smoother-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Pig collagen is collagen protein from porcine skin, found in Korean sheet masks and creams and taken as a supplement. People use it for plumper, smoother-looking, better-hydrated skin.

The idea is that collagen in a mask or cream hydrates the surface so skin looks fuller. Wikipedia notes that intact collagen is too large to enter skin, so many cosmetics use hydrolysed peptides, and that as of 2025 it reports no clinical evidence for topical or oral collagen against wrinkles. Porcine collagen itself is used in wound dressings and dental and surgical membranes.
quick.how: Most people use it as a sheet mask or cream applied to the face as part of a hydration routine, often several times a week. Supplement versions are taken by mouth alongside other skincare. Any plumping from a mask is usually a surface-hydration effect that shows up right after use.
quick.risks: As a pork-derived product it may not suit people who avoid pork. Porcine tissue has triggered immune responses in transplant research. No cosmetic safety data were found for masks or creams.

angle.text: Pig collagen goes into Korean sheet masks and creams, and into supplements, so skin is hydrated at the surface and looks plumper and smoother. Porcine collagen has established surgical uses, while cosmetic trials of masks have not been published.

tea-tree-extract.summary: Antibacterial Australian botanical in cleansers and spot treatments, used to calm blemishes and reduce breakouts.

quick.overview:
Tea tree oil and extract come from an Australian shrub and appear in cleansers and spot treatments. People use them to get fewer, smaller breakouts and clearer-looking skin.

The oil's main component, terpinen-4-ol, shows antimicrobial activity in lab tests, which is the basis for targeting blemish-causing bacteria. A 2015 Cochrane review, as summarised on Wikipedia, found one low-quality trial favouring the oil for acne lesions. Trials specific to the extract were not found.
quick.how: Used as a wash, spot treatment or leave-on product on blemish-prone areas, often alongside the rest of an acne routine. Users typically apply it over several weeks and judge results by how often new spots appear.
quick.risks: Skin irritation and allergy occur, especially with oxidised oil. Swallowing the oil is highly toxic, and a possible link to breast enlargement in boys and men has been reported.

angle.text: Tea tree oil and extract are used in cleansers and spot treatments to reduce blemish-causing bacteria, so breakouts are fewer and smaller. A Cochrane review summarised on Wikipedia found one low-quality acne trial favouring the oil.

acerola-fruit-extract.summary: Vitamin-C-rich tropical fruit extract in beauty supplements, taken for brighter, firmer-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Acerola extract comes from a tropical fruit that is among the richest natural sources of vitamin C. It is added to beauty supplements and drinks, which people take for brighter, firmer-looking skin.

Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen synthesis and an antioxidant, so the chain runs from vitamin C supply to collagen support to firmer skin. A randomized, placebo-controlled study in women aged 35 and older tested a drink containing acerola extract with collagen peptides and other nutrients, so the effect of acerola alone was not separated out.
quick.how: Taken as a powder, capsule or drink, often in blends with collagen peptides, zinc, biotin and vitamin E. It is used daily as part of a beauty-from-within routine, with skin changes judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: The fruit is a food and no cosmetic-specific safety concerns were documented in the sources reviewed. The plant's leaves have stinging hairs that can irritate skin.

angle.text: Acerola extract supplies natural vitamin C, which supports collagen and acts as an antioxidant, so skin looks brighter and firmer. The skin study available tested a multi-ingredient drink that included acerola.

orchid-extract.summary: Antioxidant orchid botanical in Asian skincare, used for fresher, younger-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Orchid extract is a botanical from several orchid species, such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis, used in Asian skincare. It is marketed as an antioxidant for fresher, younger-looking skin.

The idea is that antioxidants reduce oxidative stress in skin so it looks younger. Published work consists of cell and animal studies plus patents, for example a Phalaenopsis extract in a cell model of sun-induced pigment spots and a patent for Dendrobium chrysotoxum in anti-aging cosmetics. No human skin trial was found.
quick.how: Used as an ingredient in creams, serums and essences within an anti-aging or brightening routine. Because the term covers different species, products vary in what they contain.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to cosmetic orchid extracts were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Orchid extracts from species such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis are used in Asian skincare as antioxidants, aiming at less oxidative skin stress and a fresher, younger look. Published work consists of lab and animal studies and patents.

lotus-extract.summary: Sacred-lotus antioxidant botanical in K-beauty skincare, used for a calmer, brighter complexion.

quick.overview:
Lotus extract comes from the sacred lotus and is used in K-beauty and other skincare as an antioxidant botanical. People use it for a calmer, brighter, healthier-looking complexion.

It is thought to work through antioxidant flavonoids and related plant compounds that protect skin. Two small 2013 studies in healthy adults tested topical lotus combined with green tea on facial wrinkles and oiliness.
quick.how: Applied as part of creams, serums and masks in a daily routine, usually combined with other botanicals such as green tea.
quick.risks: No specific cosmetic safety problems were identified in the sources reviewed. Blue lotus (Nymphaea) is a different plant with its own safety assessment.

angle.text: Sacred lotus extract is used in K-beauty skincare as an antioxidant botanical that calms and protects skin for a brighter look. Two small 2013 human studies tested it combined with green tea.

green-tea-camellia-sinensis-leaf-extract.summary: Catechin-rich antioxidant in creams, serums and supplements, used for calmer, younger-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Green tea leaf extract concentrates the polyphenols of green tea, mainly catechins such as EGCG. It is a common antioxidant in creams, serums and supplements, used for calmer, younger-looking skin and fewer breakouts.

The chain is antioxidant catechins, less oxidative and sun-related stress, and calmer-looking skin. Wikipedia reports that human research has not found good evidence of benefit for most health claims, and a 2011 EFSA review judged most proposed claims, including some on UV skin protection, insufficiently supported. One topical form is an approved prescription for genital warts.
quick.how: Applied in serums and creams as a daily antioxidant step, often under sunscreen, or taken as an oral supplement. Users judge results over weeks.
quick.risks: Oral extracts have been linked to liver toxicity, mainly attributed to EGCG, and Health Canada recommended warning labels in 2017. EFSA could not set a safe dose. Rare skin reactions are reported.

angle.text: Green tea extract is a catechin-rich antioxidant used on skin and taken orally, so oxidative and sun stress are reduced and skin looks calmer and younger. It is widely studied for general health, with appearance-specific support more limited.

papaya-extract.summary: Papaya enzyme exfoliant in masks and cleansers, used for smoother, brighter-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Papaya extract is used in masks and cleansers as an enzyme exfoliant. People use it for smoother, brighter-looking skin.

Papaya latex contains papain, a protein-digesting enzyme that loosens dead surface cells, which is the basis for exfoliation. Papain is also used in meat tenderizers, wound debridement products and dental gels. No human trial of papaya extract for skin appearance was found; research covers other uses and animal studies.
quick.how: Used as a leave-on mask or rinse-off cleanser, typically once or a few times a week as a gentle alternative to acid exfoliants.
quick.risks: The FDA warned companies in 2008 to stop marketing topical papain drug products after hypersensitivity reports. People allergic to latex may also react to papaya.

angle.text: Papaya extract works as an enzyme exfoliant: papain digests protein in dead surface cells, leaving skin smoother and brighter. Trials of the extract for skin appearance were not found.

oat-extract.summary: Colloidal oat soothing ingredient for dry, irritated skin, with FDA skin-protectant status.

quick.overview:
Oat extract in skincare is mostly colloidal oatmeal or avenanthramide-standardized extract, used to calm dry, irritated skin so it looks smoother and more comfortable. It appears in sensitive-skin, baby and sun-care products.

Avenanthramides are proposed to reduce inflammation, including through NF-kappaB inhibition, and ease itch. Wikipedia states the FDA approved colloidal oatmeal as a skin protectant in 2003, and oat baths were used for itchy skin in the 19th century. Trials found for other oat extracts are mostly dietary.
quick.how: Used as creams, lotions, cleansers and bath soaks, often daily on dry or sensitive areas as part of a barrier-care routine.
quick.risks: No safety data on cosmetic oat extract were available in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Colloidal oat and oat extracts calm dry, irritated skin through avenanthramides, so skin looks smoother and less reactive. Colloidal oatmeal holds FDA skin-protectant status.

cucumber-extract.summary: Cooling, hydrating botanical in cleansers, gels and eye products for a fresh, less tired-looking face.

quick.overview:
Cucumber extract appears in gels, toners, cleansers and eye products as a cooling, soothing ingredient. People use it for a fresh feel and a less puffy, tired-looking eye area.

The raw fruit is about 95 percent water, which underlies its hydrating, cooling reputation, and manufacturers describe it as mildly hydrating and soothing. No controlled human trial in the sources reviewed has measured an effect on skin appearance. Many papers indexed as cucumber extract actually concern sea cucumbers.
quick.how: Used in eye gels, toners and masks, often chilled, as a refreshing step in a morning or evening routine.
quick.risks: Topical risks are those of any plant-based cosmetic, mainly individual irritation or allergy to the finished product. Oral toxicity and mutagenicity studies exist for a standardized extract but concern ingestion.

angle.text: Cucumber extract is a cooling, hydrating botanical in eye and face products that leaves skin fresh and soothed, so the eye area looks less tired. It is included mostly for mild hydration and feel.

chamomile-extract.summary: Calming flower extract in creams, cleansers and masks, used to make sensitive, red skin look calmer.

quick.overview:
Chamomile extract comes from daisy-like flowers and is a staple soothing ingredient in creams, cleansers and masks. People with sensitive or red skin use it for a calmer, less irritated look.

The flowers contain flavonoids such as apigenin, quercetin and luteolin, and lab studies report that chamomile preparations dampen inflammatory pathways, including COX-2, in cultured cells. Human research has mainly tested oral extracts for anxiety and sleep, and no trial in the sources reviewed tests it for a cosmetic skin outcome.
quick.how: Applied in soothing creams, toners and masks, usually daily for sensitive skin, and also taken as herbal tea.
quick.risks: People allergic to daisy-family plants such as ragweed or chrysanthemum may react. Oral use has cautions around anticoagulants and pregnancy.

angle.text: Chamomile extract is used in soothing products to reduce visible irritation, leaving sensitive skin calmer and less red. Lab studies show anti-inflammatory activity, and oral trials have focused on anxiety and sleep.

pomegranate-extract.summary: Ellagitannin-rich antioxidant extract taken or applied for a brighter, more even, healthier-looking complexion.

quick.overview:
Pomegranate extract concentrates the fruit's polyphenols, mainly ellagitannins, and is sold as a supplement and as an antioxidant in skincare. People use it for a clearer, more even, healthier-looking complexion.

Ellagitannins are converted by gut bacteria into urolithins, which are studied for anti-inflammatory activity, and polyphenols scavenge free radicals in lab assays. Most research is in cells, rodents and metabolic studies in people. A trial on skin aging and inflammation is registered, with no published result in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: Taken as a capsule or juice-based supplement or applied in serums and creams as a daily antioxidant, with changes judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: No specific safety concerns with oral extract were found in the sources reviewed. The FDA and FTC have acted against unsupported disease claims by a major juice marketer. Responses differ between people because gut microbiota differ.

angle.text: Pomegranate extract delivers ellagitannin antioxidants, taken orally or applied, so oxidative skin stress falls and skin looks brighter and healthier. Its chemistry is well studied in the lab, and a skin-aging trial is registered.

aloe-leaf-extract.summary: The classic soothing, hydrating plant gel in after-sun products and moisturizers for calmer, smoother skin.

quick.overview:
Aloe leaf extract is a staple of after-sun gels, moisturizers, sunscreens and facial products. People use it to soothe and hydrate skin so it looks calmer and smoother.

The clear inner gel is mostly water and contains the polysaccharide acemannan. Wikipedia describes the evidence for burns and wounds as conflicting, and small registered trials are mostly in oral and gum conditions. None in the sources reviewed test cosmetic appearance.
quick.how: Applied as a gel or in lotions, commonly after sun exposure or as a light daily moisturizer on irritated or dry skin.
quick.risks: Topical use in small amounts is likely safe, with allergic reactions possible. Oral latex or whole-leaf extract is linked to cramps, diarrhea and hepatitis, and regulators have acted on aloin laxatives; the cosmetic limit on anthraquinones is 50 ppm.

angle.text: Aloe gel soothes and hydrates skin, so it looks calmer and smoother after sun or irritation. Evidence on wound healing is conflicting, and its effect on appearance specifically is lightly studied.

sugarcane-extract.summary: Plant source of glycolic acid used as a gentle exfoliant for smoother, brighter skin texture.

quick.overview:
Sugarcane extract is used in skincare mainly as a plant-derived source of glycolic acid, an alpha hydroxy acid. People use it to exfoliate dull skin and get a smoother, brighter texture.

AHAs loosen surface skin cells as chemical exfoliants, and glycolic acid itself is well established in cosmetics. Products labeled sugarcane extract vary in content and strength. A separate polyphenol-rich sugarcane extract has been studied in cells and animals for antioxidant activity, and no skin-appearance trial was found.
quick.how: Used in cleansers, toners and creams as a mild exfoliating step a few times a week, usually with sunscreen during the day.
quick.risks: AHAs commonly cause mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA has warned they can increase sunburn likelihood, an effect that reverses when use stops. One anticancer paper on the polyphenol extract was retracted.

angle.text: Sugarcane extract is promoted as a natural glycolic acid source that gently exfoliates the surface, leaving skin smoother and brighter. Glycolic acid is well studied as an exfoliant, while the plant extract has not been tested for skin results.

apple-fruit-water.summary: Mild fruit-acid botanical water in some creams, used for light exfoliation and softer, fresher-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Apple fruit water is a water extract of apple used in some creams as a gentle source of fruit acids and polyphenols. People use it for light exfoliation and softer, fresher-looking skin.

The alpha hydroxy acids act as chemical exfoliants while the polyphenols are antioxidants. The one dedicated study, from 2018, described a cream with 6 percent wild apple fruit water extract said to contain 3.5 percent AHAs.
quick.how: Used as an ingredient in daily creams, usually as a mild step within a regular moisturizing routine.
quick.risks: AHAs commonly cause mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA has warned they may increase sunburn likelihood.

angle.text: Apple fruit water supplies mild fruit acids and polyphenols that lightly exfoliate and protect, so skin looks softer and fresher. The published support is a single 2018 formulation study.

turmeric-root-extract.summary: Curcumin-rich plant extract used in skincare for a brighter, more even, glowing complexion.

quick.overview:
Turmeric root extract comes from the Curcuma longa rhizome and is used in skincare as a brightening and antioxidant ingredient. People use it for a more even, glowing complexion.

Its main pigment, curcumin, has been reported in cell models to dampen TGF-beta signaling and, with another antioxidant, to reduce UV-induced oxidative damage in keratinocytes. The sources reviewed contain no human trials of topical turmeric extract for skin tone, and Wikipedia notes curcumin's instability and poor absorption.
quick.how: Applied in masks, serums and creams as part of a brightening routine, and also taken as a dietary supplement. It is also a food coloring.
quick.risks: Curcumin is a contact allergen and a strong yellow pigment that can stain. Oral use has been linked to nausea and, rarely, liver injury, and a case report describes yellow discoloration of the feet.

angle.text: Turmeric root extract is used as a brightening and antioxidant ingredient, aiming at less pigment and oxidative stress and a more even tone. Support comes mainly from cell studies.

menthyl-lactate.summary: Milder, longer-lasting menthol-derived cooling agent that gives cosmetics a fresh, refreshing feel.

quick.overview:
Menthyl lactate is an ester of menthol and lactic acid used as a cooling agent in cosmetics, fragrances and oral-care products. It gives skin products a fresh, refreshing sensation, milder and longer-lasting than menthol.

It works as a physiological coolant, so the payoff is how skin feels during use rather than a change in how it looks. No published study in the sources reviewed tests it for an appearance outcome.
quick.how: It is an ingredient in lotions, gels and after-shave type products, chosen for feel. It is used wherever a cooling sensation is wanted.
quick.risks: The main safety document in the sources is a RIFM fragrance-ingredient assessment. Little other safety literature on skincare use was found.

angle.text: Menthyl lactate is a cooling agent that makes products feel fresh and skin feel calmer while they are in use. It is valued for sensation, and no study has tested it for changes in how skin looks.

exosome-serums.summary: Vesicle-based serums used for skin regeneration, often after microneedling, for smoother, rejuvenated skin.

quick.overview:
Exosome serums contain extracellular vesicles, tiny particles cells release to signal each other. They are used for skin regeneration and rejuvenation, often after microneedling, to speed recovery and improve texture.

Vesicles carry proteins, lipids and RNA between cells, and the idea is that these signals prompt skin cells to repair and renew. Extracellular vesicles are an active research area, but a couple of registered trials turned up with no published results for cosmetic use.
quick.how: Applied as a serum, most often right after microneedling or other procedures, as part of a recovery and rejuvenation routine.
quick.risks: Researchers note that isolating and measuring vesicles is difficult and standardization is lacking, so products vary. No regulatory or adverse-event data for cosmetic products were in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Exosome serums carry cell signals meant to drive skin repair, applied after microneedling for faster recovery and smoother, rejuvenated skin. The biology is active in the lab, and published human skin data are very limited.

mesenchymal-stem-cell-conditioned-media.summary: Stem-cell secretome liquid in serums and post-procedure treatments for skin repair and rejuvenation.

quick.overview:
Mesenchymal stem cell conditioned media is the liquid in which stem cells have grown, containing the growth factors and vesicles they secrete. It appears in serums and post-procedure treatments for skin regeneration and a smoother, rejuvenated look.

The secreted factors are thought to signal nearby cells, for example promoting fibroblast migration and dampening inflammation in cell models. Most research is lab and animal wound-healing work, and early-phase human trials are registered for conditions such as chronic ulcers and keloids.
quick.how: Applied as a serum, often after microneedling or other procedures, as a cell-free alternative to stem cell therapy.
quick.risks: Composition varies between preparations. A laboratory study reported MSC-derived chemokines promoting tumor-cell invasion, and no long-term cosmetic safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Stem-cell conditioned media carry growth factors and vesicles meant to signal skin repair and collagen support for smoother, rejuvenated skin. Lab and animal work is extensive, and human trials are early-phase.

fibroblast-growth-factor-fgf.summary: Wound-repair growth factor added to anti-aging serums for firmer, smoother-looking skin.

quick.overview:
FGFs are signaling proteins that drive cell growth and wound repair, and FGF2 (bFGF) is the form most discussed for skin. Some anti-aging serums contain growth factors of this type, aimed at firmer, smoother-looking skin.

FGFs bind receptors on cells and promote fibroblast proliferation, blood vessel formation and granulation tissue, which is why more collagen and repair is the hoped-for result. Wikipedia states FGF2 has been shown to enhance tissue repair in burns, skin grafts and ulcers. No trials of topical FGF serums for wrinkles were found.
quick.how: Used as a topical serum within an anti-aging routine, often alongside other peptides and growth-factor products.
quick.risks: Overactive FGF signaling is associated with several diseases. Safety of cosmetic use was not covered in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Topical FGF is added to anti-aging serums to stimulate fibroblasts and new collagen for firmer, smoother skin. It is well studied in wound repair, and human cosmetic trials for wrinkles were not found.

anagain.summary: Pea-sprout extract in cosmetic hair serums, used for thicker, fuller-looking scalp hair.

quick.overview:
Anagain is a branded extract from pea sprouts used in over-the-counter hair serums and lotions. People use it for thicker, fuller-looking scalp hair, often discussed alongside Redensyl, Capixyl and Baicapil.

The idea is that it shifts signals that favor follicle activity. A short communication in Phytotherapy Research reported that a fluid with 2% pea sprout extract changed expression of hair-growth genes in 10 volunteers. A 2025 review lists it among cosmeceutical hair-loss actives.
quick.how: Applied as a leave-on scalp serum or lotion on a regular schedule, often alongside other hair-growth actives, with results judged over months.
quick.risks: No safety problems were identified in the sources reviewed, though no large safety data exist. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved hair-loss drug.

angle.text: Anagain is a pea-sprout extract in hair serums, meant to favor follicle activity for thicker-looking hair. Support is a small 10-person gene-expression study.
